claim: Adolescence is a common time for initiation of alcohol use and development of alcohol use disorders.
source: Adolescence is a common time for initiation of alcohol use and development of alcohol use disorders.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about adolescent behavior patterns.

claim: The study investigated neuroanatomical predictors for trajectories of future alcohol use based on a novel voxel-wise whole-brain structural equation modeling framework.
source: The present study investigates neuroanatomical predictors for trajectories of future alcohol use based on a novel voxel-wise whole-brain structural equation modeling framework.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study as stated in the abstract.

claim: The study analyzed 1814 healthy adolescents from the IMAGEN sample.
source: In 1814 healthy adolescents of the IMAGEN sample, the Alcohol Use Disorder Identification Test (AUDIT) was acquired at three measurement occasions across five years.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sample size and composition in the abstract.

claim: The Alcohol Use Disorder Identification Test (AUDIT) was acquired at three measurement occasions across five years.
source: In 1814 healthy adolescents of the IMAGEN sample, the Alcohol Use Disorder Identification Test (AUDIT) was acquired at three measurement occasions across five years.
evidence: This describes the data collection protocol as stated in the abstract.

claim: Higher grey-matter volumes in the caudate nucleus at age 14 years were predictive of stronger increase in alcohol use score over 5 years.
source: Higher grey-matter volumes in the caudate nucleus and the left cerebellum at age 14 years were predictive of stronger increase in alcohol use score over 5 years.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by the whole-brain analysis results.

claim: Higher grey-matter volumes in the left cerebellum at age 14 years were predictive of stronger increase in alcohol use score over 5 years.
source: Higher grey-matter volumes in the caudate nucleus and the left cerebellum at age 14 years were predictive of stronger increase in alcohol use score over 5 years.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by the whole-brain analysis results.

claim: The study is the first to demonstrate the feasibility of running separate voxel-wise structural equation models.
source: The study is the first to demonstrate the feasibility of running separate voxel-wise structural equation models thereby opening new avenues for data analysis in brain imaging.
evidence: This is a methodological claim stated in the abstract about the novelty of the approach.

claim: The period of adolescence coincides with substantial behavioural changes together with structural and functional brain development.
source: Importantly, the period of adolescence coincides with substantial behavioural changes together with structural and functional brain development.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Cortico-striatal regions play an important role in the regulation of behaviour and might therefore play a role in progress and maintenance of habits such as drinking.
source: Cortico-striatal regions play an important role in the regulation of behaviour and might therefore play a role in progress and maintenance of habits such as drinking (Heinz, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heinz, 2002.

claim: Drug addiction involves dysfunctions of brain circuitry related to the neurotransmitter dopamine that lead to alterations in both impulsive and compulsive behaviour.
source: In particular, it has been proposed that drug addiction involves dysfunctions of brain circuitry related to the neurotransmitter dopamine that lead to alterations in both impulsive and compulsive behaviour (Koob and Kreek, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koob and Kreek, 2007.

claim: Early exposure to drugs may alter brain development during adolescence which may set the stage for cognitive problems in adulthood.
source: Since early exposure to drugs may alter brain development during adolescence this may set the stage for cognitive problems in adulthood, which translate into behavioral consequences throughout life (Jacobus and Tapert, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jacobus and Tapert, 2013.

claim: Reward-related brain activation aided in the prediction of early-onset drinking in adolescents at age 14 years.
source: Nees and colleagues reported that reward-related brain activation aided in the prediction of early-onset drinking in adolescents at age 14 years in a subset of the data used in the present paper (Nees et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nees et al., 2012.

claim: Teens classified as transitioning to heavy alcohol use by age 18 had less BOLD activation in frontal, temporal, and parietal cortices in a response inhibition task.
source: In a functional imaging study on youth of age 12–14 years, prior to initiation of alcohol use, it was found that teens classified as transitioning to heavy alcohol use by age 18 had less blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) activation in frontal, temporal, and parietal cortices in a response inhibition task (Norman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Norman et al., 2011.

claim: Brain differences present early during adolescence may leave certain youth vulnerable to addictive behaviors.
source: These reports support the notion that brain differences present early during adolescence may leave certain youth vulnerable to addictive behaviors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies (Nees et al., 2012; Norman et al., 2011).

claim: A linear growth model demonstrated better fit to alcohol use vs. non-use than an intercept-only model.
source: In the discrete part of the model, a linear growth model demonstrated better fit to alcohol use vs. non-use than an intercept-only model, Δχ2 (Koob and Kreek, 2007) (3, N = 1814)=653.63, p<0.001.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the model comparison analysis.

claim: Inclusion of a quadratic growth factor did not improve model fit for the discrete part of the model.
source: Inclusion of a quadratic growth factor did not improve model fit, Δχ2 (Koob and Kreek, 2007) (1, N = 1814)=−0.74, p=0.390, therefore we refrained from a quadratic growth factor.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the model comparison analysis.

claim: A linear growth model demonstrated a better fit to alcohol use scores than an intercept-only model for the continuous part of the model.
source: In the continuous part of the model, a linear growth model likewise demonstrated a better fit to alcohol use scores than an intercept-only model, Δχ2 (Koob and Kreek, 2007)(3, N = 1814)=860.58, p<0.001.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the model comparison analysis.

claim: Inclusion of a quadratic growth factor did not improve model fit for the continuous part of the model.
source: Inclusion of a quadratic growth factor did not improve model fit, Δχ2 (Koob and Kreek, 2007)(1, N = 1814)=−0.58, p=0.450.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the model comparison analysis.

claim: The final model on the clinical data demonstrated an acceptable model fit with χ2 = 444, df = 65, RMSEA = 0.057, CFI = 0.785, SRMR = 0.065.
source: The final model on the clinical data, not yet including the brain data (since this varied for each voxel of the brain) demonstrated an acceptable model fit, χ2 = 444, df = 65, RMSEA = 0.057, CFI = 0.785, SRMR = 0.065.
evidence: This is a statistical finding reporting model fit indices.

claim: Intercepts were significantly different from zero for both parts of the model.
source: Concerning the latent intercept and slope for both parts of the model, intercepts were significantly different from zero and variances of the intercepts for both parts of the model were significant, suggesting significant interindividual heterogeneity around the estimated mean level of alcohol drinking use vs. non-use and the alcohol use score at age 14 (for estimates see Table 2).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the latent growth curve model analysis.

claim: Variances of the intercepts for both parts of the model were significant, suggesting significant interindividual heterogeneity around the estimated mean level of alcohol drinking use vs. non-use and the alcohol use score at age 14.
source: Concerning the latent intercept and slope for both parts of the model, intercepts were significantly different from zero and variances of the intercepts for both parts of the model were significant, suggesting significant interindividual heterogeneity around the estimated mean level of alcohol drinking use vs. non-use and the alcohol use score at age 14 (for estimates see Table 2).
evidence: This is a statistical finding and interpretation from the latent growth curve model analysis.

claim: The covariance between the intercepts of the two parts of the model was 0.124, p<0.001, indicating that adolescents with a higher propensity to engage in alcohol drinking also engaged in it more frequently and vice versa.
source: The covariance between the intercepts of the two parts of the model was 0.124, p<0.001, indicating that adolescents with a higher propensity to engage in alcohol drinking also engaged in it more frequently and vice versa.
evidence: This is a statistical finding and interpretation from the model analysis.

claim: The estimated mean of the slope for the continuous part of the model was not significantly different from zero, indicating that, on average, no change in drinking habits emerged over time.
source: For the continuous part of the model the estimated mean of the slope was not significantly different from zero, indicating that, on average, no change in drinking habits emerged over time.
evidence: This is a statistical finding and interpretation from the model analysis.

claim: The variance of the slope for the continuous part of the model was significantly different from zero, indicating interindividual differences in change of drinking behaviour between participants.
source: However, the variance was significantly different from zero, indicating interindividual differences in change of drinking behaviour between participants.
evidence: This is a statistical finding and interpretation from the model analysis.

claim: For the discrete part of the model both the mean and the variance of the slope were significantly different from zero, indicating change on average as well as interindividually.
source: For the discrete part of the model both the mean and the variance of the slope were significantly different from zero, indicating change on average as well as interindividually.
evidence: This is a statistical finding and interpretation from the model analysis.

claim: The positive mean of the slope for the discrete part indicated an increasing propensity for drinking across time.
source: The positive mean of the slope indicated an increasing propensity for drinking across time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical finding from the model analysis.

claim: Intercept and slope covaried significantly (−0.033, p<0.001) within the discrete part of the model.
source: Intercept and slope covaried significantly (−0.033, p<0.001) within the discrete part of the model, however, numerically the correlation coefficient was so small that we do not think the association necessitates in-depth interpretation.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the model analysis.

claim: No significant correlation emerged between intercept and slope for the continuous part of the model, indicating that a relation between alcohol use score at age 14 and change in this behavior was not captured in our model.
source: No significant correlation emerged between intercept and slope for the continuous part of the model, indicating that a relation between alcohol use score at age 14 and change in this behavior was not captured in our model.
evidence: This is a statistical finding and interpretation from the model analysis.

claim: A positive association was found within bilateral caudate nucleus (around −14, 24, 7 and 17, 24, 6) where higher grey matter volume predicts greater change in alcohol use scores (p<0.001, cluster >100 voxels).
source: We found a positive association within bilateral caudate nucleus (around −14, 24, 7 and 17, 24, 6) and left cerebellum (Lobule VIII/IX, around −16,–53, −56), where higher grey matter volume predicts greater change in alcohol use scores (p<0.001, cluster >100 voxels, Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the whole-brain voxel-wise analysis, also shown in Figure 3.

claim: A positive association was found within left cerebellum (Lobule VIII/IX, around −16,–53, −56) where higher grey matter volume predicts greater change in alcohol use scores (p<0.001, cluster >100 voxels).
source: We found a positive association within bilateral caudate nucleus (around −14, 24, 7 and 17, 24, 6) and left cerebellum (Lobule VIII/IX, around −16,–53, −56), where higher grey matter volume predicts greater change in alcohol use scores (p<0.001, cluster >100 voxels, Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the whole-brain voxel-wise analysis, also shown in Figure 3.

claim: The same analysis on log-transformed data produced almost identical results.
source: We repeated the same analysis on log-transformed data, to address the problem of skewness in the data with almost identical results.
evidence: This is a robustness check reported in the results.

claim: The same analysis on white matter probability maps did not result in any significant clusters.
source: The same analysis on white matter probability maps did not result in any significant clusters.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the whole-brain analysis.

claim: Repeating the same analyses when investigating a regression path between white or grey matter voxels and the change in alcohol use vs. non-use did not result in any significant clusters.
source: Neither did repeating the same analyses when investigating a regression path between white or grey matter voxels and the change in alcohol use vs. non-use.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the whole-brain analysis.

claim: The whole-brain analysis while predicting the latent intercept of the continuous part of the model did not result in any significant clusters for either white or grey matter maps.
source: Moreover, we conducted the same whole-brain analysis while predicting the latent intercept of the continuous part of the model, which reflects how high individuals score on AUDIT on average. Here also no significant clusters emerged, neither for white nor grey matter maps.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the whole-brain analysis.

claim: Caudate and cerebellum have been described as undergoing changes over the lifetime that resemble an inverted U-shape in gray matter volume that peaks during adolescence.
source: Caudate and cerebellum have been described as undergoing changes over the lifetime that resemble an inverted U-shape in gray matter volume that peaks during adolescence (Durston et al., 2001; Brenhouse and Andersen, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Durston et al., 2001 and Brenhouse and Andersen, 2011.

claim: On a longitudinal data set the changes of caudate over the course of adolescence were the smallest in comparison to other subcortical brain structures.
source: However, on a longitudinal data set the changes of caudate over the course of adolescence were the smallest in comparison to other subcortical brain structures with caudate, putamen and nucleus accumbens peaking at earlier ages than amygdala and hippocampus (Goddings et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Goddings et al., 2014.

claim: Caudate, putamen and nucleus accumbens peak at earlier ages than amygdala and hippocampus.
source: However, on a longitudinal data set the changes of caudate over the course of adolescence were the smallest in comparison to other subcortical brain structures with caudate, putamen and nucleus accumbens peaking at earlier ages than amygdala and hippocampus (Goddings et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Goddings et al., 2014.

claim: Females seem to show a peak in caudate volume around age 11 years and males seem to show a decrease in caudate volume over adolescence.
source: In tendency females seem to show a peak around age 11 years and males seem to show a decrease in caudate volume over adolescence (Goddings et al., 2014; Brain Development Cooperative Group, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goddings et al., 2014 and Brain Development Cooperative Group, 2012.

claim: One study reported decreases in cerebellum volume across adolescence.
source: The pattern of changes in the cerebellum seem less clear with one study reporting decreases across adolescence (Ostby et al., 2009) and another showing an inverse U-shape pattern with a peak around 15 years of age (Brain Development Cooperative Group, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ostby et al., 2009.

claim: Another study showed an inverse U-shape pattern in cerebellum volume with a peak around 15 years of age.
source: The pattern of changes in the cerebellum seem less clear with one study reporting decreases across adolescence (Ostby et al., 2009) and another showing an inverse U-shape pattern with a peak around 15 years of age (Brain Development Cooperative Group, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brain Development Cooperative Group, 2012.

claim: At baseline (12–17 years of age) participants who transitioned into heavy drinking after 3 years showed smaller left cingulate, pars triangularis, and rostral anterior cingulate volume, and less right cerebellar white matter volumes.
source: One study on 40 adolescents using FreeSurfer showed that at baseline (12–17 years of age) participants who transitioned into heavy drinking after 3 years showed smaller left cingulate, pars triangularis, and rostral anterior cingulate volume, and less right cerebellar white matter volumes (Squeglia et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Squeglia et al., 2014.

claim: Participants who had their first drink during puberty showed increases in brain activation in caudate nucleus at reward delivery as compared to those who started after puberty.
source: Other studies focussed on activation of the striatum, for example during an fMRI reward paradigm, reporting increases in brain activation in caudate nucleus at reward delivery in participants who had their first drink during puberty as compared to those who started after puberty (Boecker-Schlier et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boecker-Schlier et al., 2017.

claim: Transitioners to heavy drinking showed higher activation in bilateral caudate nucleus, orbitofrontal cortex medial frontal cortex/anterior cingulate and left insula in a cue-reactivity paradigm showing alcohol stimuli.
source: In a cue-reactivity paradigm showing alcohol stimuli, transitioners showed higher activation in bilateral caudate nucleus, orbitofrontal cortex medial frontal cortex/anterior cingulate and left insula (Dager et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dager et al., 2014.

claim: The cluster in caudate nucleus and cerebellum found to be predictive of the future changes in alcohol use scores were not related to the mean level of alcohol use scores in each individual.
source: Of note, it is very interesting that the cluster in caudate nucleus and cerebellum found to be predictive of the future changes in alcohol use scores were not related to the mean level of alcohol use scores in each individual, since we observe no significant regions in the analysis where the latent intercept of the continuous part of the model predicts the respective brain voxels.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings comparing different analyses.

claim: The grey matter volume in caudate nucleus and cerebellum has a value in predicting changes, but not the average alcohol use in general at the timepoint analysed.
source: This indicates that the grey matter volume in caudate nucleus and cerebellum has a value in predicting changes, but not the average alcohol use in general at the timepoint analysed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Preventive measures at age 14 should focus on the development of alcohol use rather than on drinking habits at the age of 14.
source: On the basis of the present analyses, one might argue that preventive measures at this age should focus on the development of alcohol use rather than on drinking habits at the age of 14, as the results suggest that specific characteristics of those brain regions prepare the ground for future alcohol consumption.
evidence: This is a speculative recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Brain data is not indicative for the prognosis when individuals start drinking.
source: The fact that the brain-based prediction of the latent slope of the dichotomous part of the model showed no significant resulting clusters indicates that, using the presented methods, brain data is not indicative for the prognosis when individuals start drinking.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the negative findings from the analysis.

claim: Brain information (at age 14 years) added only moderately in the prediction of binge drinking at age 16 years.
source: In this sense, the present results could be regarded as in line with a previous publication from the IMAGEN data set (Whelan et al., 2014) in which it was shown that brain information (at age 14 years) added only moderately in the prediction of binge drinking at age 16 years.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Whelan et al., 2014.

claim: Only diffuse regions added to the prediction of initiation of alcohol use during adolescence in a different data set.
source: In a different data set (Squeglia et al., 2017), likewise only diffuse regions added to the prediction of initiation of alcohol use during adolescence.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Squeglia et al., 2017.

claim: Brain characteristics might not be the key factor in explaining the start of alcohol consumption in adolescence.
source: While we learned from previous studies that brain characteristics might not be the key factor in explaining the start of alcohol consumption in adolescence, we learn from the present study that brain structural characteristics are of relevance when considering the development of alcohol use in adolescence.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current study and previous literature.

claim: Brain structural characteristics are of relevance when considering the development of alcohol use in adolescence.
source: While we learned from previous studies that brain characteristics might not be the key factor in explaining the start of alcohol consumption in adolescence, we learn from the present study that brain structural characteristics are of relevance when considering the development of alcohol use in adolescence.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current study findings.

claim: A recent meta-analysis on brain imaging studies revealed consistency in increases within bilateral striatum when comparing psychiatric patients to controls.
source: Interestingly, a recent meta-analysis on brain imaging studies focussing on brain structural alterations across psychiatric disorders has revealed consistency in increases within bilateral striatum when comparing psychiatric patients to controls (Goodkind et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Goodkind et al., 2015.

claim: Up to now structural equation modeling on brain imaging data has been conducted solely based on data derived from regions of interest (ROIs).
source: To our knowledge up to now structural equation modeling on brain imaging data has been conducted solely based on data derived from regions of interest (ROIs) (Kievit et al., 2014; Kühn et al., 2017; McArdle et al., 2004; Raz et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kievit et al., 2014; Kühn et al., 2017; McArdle et al., 2004; Raz et al., 2005.

claim: The present study demonstrates the feasibility of running separate structural equation models for each and every voxel of the brain.
source: The present study demonstrates the feasibility of running separate structural equation models for each and every voxel of the brain and therefore plot the voxel-wise results of structural equation models back into brain space.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about what the study accomplished.

claim: The voxel-wise SEM approach can be applied to all models in an SEM context, not just growth curve models.
source: This approach is not restricted to growth curve models but can be applied to all models in an SEM context.
evidence: This is a claim about the generalizability of the methodological approach.

claim: The voxel-wise SEM approach can be applied to measurement models to relate brain structure or function to latent factors representing shared variance of different performance measures.
source: It can for example also be applied to measurement models, in order to relate brain structure or function not only to a separate task performance measure but rather to the latent factor representing the shared variance of a set of different performance measures from the same cognitive domain.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential applications of the method.

claim: The study used data of 1794 healthy 14-year-old adolescents (mean age = 14.4, SD = 0.45 years; 54% males) recruited within the IMAGEN project.
source: We used data of 1794 healthy 14-year-old adolescents (mean age = 14.4, SD = 0.45 years; 54% males) who were recruited within the scope of the IMAGEN project, a European multi-centre genetic-neuroimaging study in adolescence (Schumann et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the study sample and is supported by a citation to Schumann et al., 2010.

claim: At age 16–17 years, retest data was present for 1439 participants (mean age = 16.6, SD = 0.64 years; 55% males).
source: At the time of analyses reported here (age 14 years), retest data at age 16–17 years was present for 1439 participants (mean age = 16.6, SD = 0.64 years; 55% males) and at age 19 years for 1284 participants (mean age = 19.0, SD = 0.77 years; 53% males).
evidence: This describes the follow-up sample characteristics.

claim: At age 19 years, retest data was present for 1284 participants (mean age = 19.0, SD = 0.77 years; 53% males).
source: At the time of analyses reported here (age 14 years), retest data at age 16–17 years was present for 1439 participants (mean age = 16.6, SD = 0.64 years; 55% males) and at age 19 years for 1284 participants (mean age = 19.0, SD = 0.77 years; 53% males).
evidence: This describes the follow-up sample characteristics.

claim: Written informed consent was obtained from all participants as well as from their legal guardians.
source: Written informed consent was obtained from all participants as well as from their legal guardians.
evidence: This describes the ethical procedures of the study.

claim: The study was approved by all local ethics committees separately.
source: The study was approved by all local ethics committees separately (in Germany this was accomplished by the medical ethics committee of the University of Heidelberg, reference number: 2007-024N-MA) and approved by the head teachers of the respective schools.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval of the study.

claim: Participants with a medical condition or neurological disorders were excluded.
source: Participants with a medical condition or neurological disorders were excluded.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria of the study.

claim: All participating subjects were assessed by means of self-rating and two external ratings (by their parents and a psychiatrist specialized in pediatrics) based on ICD-10 as well as DSM-IV.
source: All participating subjects were assessed by means of self-rating and two external ratings (by their parents and a psychiatrist specialized in pediatrics) based on ICD-10 as well as DSM-IV (The Development and Well-Being Assessment Interview, DAWBA; Goodman et al., 2000).
evidence: This describes the assessment procedures and is supported by a citation to Goodman et al., 2000.

claim: Structural MRI was performed on 3 Tesla scanners from three manufacturers (Siemens: five sites; Philips: two sites; and General Electric: two sites).
source: Structural MRI was performed on 3 Tesla scanners from three manufacturers (Siemens: five sites; Philips: two sites; and General Electric: two sites).
evidence: This describes the MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: High-resolution anatomical MRIs were obtained using a three-dimensional magnetization prepared gradient-echo (MPRAGE) sequence based on the ADNI protocol modified for the IMAGEN study to give a 1.1 × 1.1 × 1.1 mm3 voxel size.
source: These high-resolution anatomical MRIs were obtained using a three-dimensional magnetization prepared gradient-echo (MPRAGE) sequence based on the ADNI protocol (http://adni.loni.usc.edu/methods/documents/mri-protocols/; modified for the IMAGEN study to give a 1.1 × 1.1 × 1.1 mm3 voxel size).
evidence: This describes the MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Structural MR data of 2072 adolescents were available for the present report.
source: For the present report, structural MR data of 2072 adolescents were available.
evidence: This describes the available data for analysis.

claim: All participants where the image quality was suboptimal, most likely due to movement, were excluded.
source: We excluded all participants where the image quality was suboptimal, most likely due to movement.
evidence: This describes the quality control procedures.

claim: The visual quality control was carried out by 10 independent raters.
source: The visual quality control was carried out by 10 independent raters.
evidence: This describes the quality control procedures.

claim: Structural data acquired at age 14 years was preprocessed by means of the VBM8 toolbox and SPM8 with default parameters.
source: Structural data acquired at age 14 years was preprocessed by means of the VBM8 toolbox (http://dbm.neuro.uni-jena.de/vbm.html) and SPM8 (http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm) with default parameters.
evidence: This describes the preprocessing methods.

claim: The VBM8 toolbox involves bias correction, tissue classification and affine registration.
source: The VBM8 toolbox involves bias correction, tissue classification and affine registration.
evidence: This describes the preprocessing steps.

claim: Images were smoothed with a FWHM (full-width at half maximum) kernel of 8 mm.
source: Images were smoothed with a FWHM (full-width at half maximum) kernel of 8 mm.
evidence: This describes the preprocessing parameters.

claim: Analyses were conducted within a structural equation modeling (SEM) framework using MPlus and R.
source: Analyses were conducted within a structural equation modeling (SEM) framework using MPlus and R.
evidence: This describes the analysis software and framework.

claim: A two-part latent growth curve model was implemented since the AUDIT scores were zero inflated.
source: We implemented a two-part latent growth curve model (Muthen, 2001; Olsen and Schafer, 2001) since the AUDIT scores were zero inflated.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach and is supported by citations to Muthen, 2001 and Olsen and Schafer, 2001.

claim: In a two-part latent growth curve model, zeros are valid values with its own meaning and not just proxies for missingness.
source: In a two-part latent growth curve model, zeros are valid values with its own meaning and not just proxies for missingness.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the analytical approach.

claim: Information that is contained by zeros and the specific values of the non-zeros is qualitatively different and might even be differentially influenced by covariates.
source: Information that is contained by zeros and the specific values of the non-zeros is qualitatively different and might even be differentially influenced by covariates (cf., Olsen and Schafer, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Olsen and Schafer, 2001.

claim: In the two-part latent growth curve model, the presence or absence of a behavior and, if present, the manifestation of a specific behavior can be modeled simultaneously in one model.
source: In a two-part latent growth curve model, the presence or absence of a behavior and, if present, the manifestation of a specific behavior can be modeled simultaneously in one model.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the analytical approach.

claim: Maximum Likelihood estimator was used for the analyses.
source: We used Maximum Likelihood estimator for our analyses.
evidence: This describes the statistical estimation method.

claim: The study controlled for the effects of age at baseline, sex, total brain volume (TBV) and site onto the slope of the continuous part of the growth model.
source: We controlled for the effects of age at baseline, sex, total brain volume (TBV) and site (by dummy coding eight of all nine neuroimaging sites, for simplicity we represent this by only one manifest variable in Figure 2) onto the slope of the continuous part of the growth model.
evidence: This describes the covariates included in the model.

claim: Values of the CFI above 0.90 denote a well-fitting model.
source: Values of the CFI above 0.90 denote a well-fitting model, whereas for the RMSEA and the SRMR values less than 0.08 may be interpreted as acceptable model-fit.
evidence: This describes the criteria for evaluating model fit.

claim: For the RMSEA and the SRMR values less than 0.08 may be interpreted as acceptable model-fit.
source: Values of the CFI above 0.90 denote a well-fitting model, whereas for the RMSEA and the SRMR values less than 0.08 may be interpreted as acceptable model-fit.
evidence: This describes the criteria for evaluating model fit.

claim: Separate two-part growth mixture models were run for each and every voxel of the brain.
source: For this purpose, we ran separate two-part growth mixture models for each and every voxel of the brain and repeated this analyses for the grey and white matter maps separately.
evidence: This describes the voxel-wise analysis approach.

claim: The resulting maps were thresholded with a threshold of p<0.001 and a cluster threshold of k > 100.
source: Finally, we thresholded the resulting maps with a threshold of p<0.001 and a cluster threshold of k > 100.
evidence: This describes the statistical thresholding applied to the results.
